CHURCH,,,Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege, we look upon your honour as the protector and custodian of the rights and privileges of members of parliament. These rights and privileges cannot be taken away from an hon. member either by you or by your deputy, by the government or by anybody else. As a private member I wish to direct the attention of your honour to a very undignified incident which occurred in this chamber yesterday afternoon while your honour was present. I had not intended to take part in the debate in committee of ways and

means, but at five minutes to six I rose in my place when the hon. member for North Huron (Mr. Deachman) had concluded. I had spoken for about three minutes when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), who is supposed to show hon. members on this side of the house some courtesy-

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Thomas Langton Church,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b4773d7c-fb30-477a-9d14-c076e60905ac&Language=E&Section=ALL

,,,Some hon. MEMBERS:,
1085538,ca.proc.d.1936-03-19.2.3,1936-03-19,b4773d7c-fb30-477a-9d14-c076e60905ac,ca.m.9274,Mr. CHURCH:,,PRIVILEGE-MR. CHURCH,,,A member of parliament

is here as the free representative of the people and he has rights, prerogatives and privileges which cannot be taken away from him by the government of the day, even though they may have a majority of one or two hundred. The chairman pro tempore was presiding over the committee, but I do not know how he got in the chair. I do not think he had any right to be there, under the rules as I see them, and I have some authorities on this matter. While I was on my feet speaking the Minister of Finance before six o'clock rose in his place and moved that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again. The minister may have been able to get away with things like that in the Saskatchewan legislature, but he is not going to get away with them here. I ask your honour to protect the rights, privileges and prerogatives which I have as a private member of this house. I was elected by the constituents of Broadview' and I want to assert the rights, the privileges, the functions and the prerogatives which every private member has here under the British constitution. We are supposed to have free parliamentary institutions in Canada but it has not been so, and they have been curtailed during the past few years; this principle has been departed from with the result that there is no longer any freedom in the press, in the legislatures, in the pulpits or in the universities. I wish to protest, as strongly as I can, against it. No wonder we have seen, in the past few years, the decay and decline of the House of Commons in Canada.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Thomas Langton Church,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b4773d7c-fb30-477a-9d14-c076e60905ac&Language=E&Section=ALL

CHURCH,,,Mr. Speaker, I should like to call your attention to the fact that when I was presiding in the committee of ways and means yesterday afternoon I made a sign to the hon. gentleman who has just spoken (Mr. Church) that a motion was before the chair that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again. Unfortunately the hon. gentleman suffers from deafness and did not understand what I said or see the sign that I made to him. I submit that I was perfectly in order in taking the action that I did.
Unemployment

Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance): Mr. Speaker, if it will help to ease matters at all, may I apologize most sincerely to the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) if any action on my part hurt his feelings in any way. Certainly such was not my intention. I thought and I still think that I was within the rules of the house when at a few minutes to six o'clock I moved that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again in order that such report could be made to Your Honour before you left the chair at six o'clock, which I think is the correct procedure. I had no intention whatever of taking away any privilege from my hon. friend. If I did succeed in taking away three minutes of his speech I will undertake to try to help him get it back on some future occasion. I might say however that I doubt whether the hon. member really has much complaint. As a rule, because of his little infirmity, it is quite difficult to appeal to Your Honour on a point of order when the hon. member has the floor, and in that regard he receives, I think, considerable latitude from his opponents. I think therefore he might forgive me just this once if I have hurt his feelings.

Minister of Pensions (Mr. Power), and on
his behalf, I move that the house go into committee to-morrow to consider the following proposed resolution standing in his name:

That it is expedient to bring in a measure to provide under the War Veterans' Allowance Act for special consideration for certain veterans not having attained the age of sixty, but having attained the age of fifty-five, who by reason of disability, pre-ageing and general unfitness, are incapable of maintaining themselves; to provide for continuation of part of the allowance to dependents of certain veterans admitted for treatment to departmental institutions; to substitute a war veterans' allowance board for a war veterans' allowance committee and to provide for the continuance in office of the members of the committee as members of the board and for their salaries, superannuation and pension, and to provide a more complete definition of the board's powers.
His Excellency the Governor General, having been made acquainted with the subject matter of this resolution, recommends it to the favourable consideration of the house.

Minister of Pensions (Mr. Power) and on his behalf I move that the house go into committee to-morrow to consider the following proposed resolution standing in his name:

1085557,ca.proc.d.1936-03-19.7.1.2,1936-03-19,b4773d7c-fb30-477a-9d14-c076e60905ac,ca.m.9274,Mr. T. L. CHURCH (Broadview):,,BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT,EFFECT UPON LARGE MUNICIPALITIES OF PROPOSED AMENDMENTS RESPECTING TAXATION,,I wish

to ask the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) a question. On to-day's order paper there is a notice of motion respecting proposed changes in the British North America Act to add greatly to the powers of provincial authority. The municipalities, particularly the larger ones, may be very seriously interfered with by this proposed resolution to give the provinces the right to raise revenues not only by direct taxation within the province but also in regard to indirect taxation. I especially refer to the sales tax. Will the Minister of Justice be kind enough to give the larger municipalities an opportunity of being heard first as to the way in which a measure such as this is likely to affect the taxpayers and municipal institutions in the provinces and interfere with their present powers of taxation?

United States tariff-1604. Agricultural implements: Ploughs, tooth or disc harrows, headers, harvesters, reapers, combination
harvesting and' threshing machines, agricultural drills and planters, mowers, horse-rakes, and cultivators, whether in whole or in parts, including repair parts, free.",,,,
1085562,ca.proc.d.1936-03-19.8.1.2,1936-03-19,b4773d7c-fb30-477a-9d14-c076e60905ac,ca.m.9274,Mr. CHURCH:,,WAYS AND MEANS,CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT,,"Mr. Chairman, I will not

detain the committee this afternoon for longer than five or ten minutes. This item concerns implements going out of Canada. I wish to say a few words on behalf of workers in the city of Toronto and elsewhere who are engaged in the Massey-Harris, Cockshutt Plow, International Harvester and other factories producing implements. This industry was built up under a protective tariff, and these agricultural implements may go into the United States free of duty. We have always had some kind of protective duty; it is now down to about 12J per cent, which is practically no duty at all when you figure out the taxes which the industry has to pay. The lot of these workers was referred to by me the other night on the motion of the hon. member for St. Mary (Mr. Deslauriers), and I repeat that these industries have practically no protection at all.

I want to say a few words on behalf of the great mass of the intelligent electorate who are not concerned with the game of the ins and the outs as the party politicians play it to-day, but who wish to reassert the supremacy of the national over the party interest. It is the duty of a member of parliament when the question of tariff on agricultural implements arises to assert the supremacy of parliament and the right of the private member to function along the lines of our constitutional government in order to help rebuild the structure of our social and economic order. As I see it, the country is sick and tired of the way we play this game of politics in the committee of ways and means. We want a new set of rules for this game when we see that one member of the government can go down to Washington over the heads of parliament and sign, seal and deliver a treaty between the two high contracting parties, the President of the United States and the Prime Minister of this country, parliament and this committee are just going around in a circle.

The Massey industry to which I refer has done a great deal to build up the city of Toronto. Owing to the depression and to the loss of export markets in Great Britain, Australia, and many other places, and economic nationalism, the implement industry now in Canada is very much under a cloud. I am not here to plead the cause of the agricultural implement manufacturers; they have never been any particular friends of mine. I am here as a member of parliament to protect the home market and save it for our workers.
Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement

We in this small corner of the house are called Conservatives. What we wish to conserve is the interest of the workers who are engaged in this industry in the home market which has provided them with a certain amount of employment all these years. According to statistics there were fifteen thousand of them engaged, in good times, in the agricultural implement industry when I last addressed the house on May 5, 1924, for protection on their behalf.

The people of the prairie provinces have more to fear from the grain exchange and the grain combine and the transportation combine and the elevator combine west of the great lakes than from the manufacturers east of the great lakes. As regards this particular reciprocity pact, as I see it, a 12J per cent duty has cut down protection so far that you might as well let it wither away altogether. I do not know what is going to become of these implement workers.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Thomas Langton Church,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b4773d7c-fb30-477a-9d14-c076e60905ac&Language=E&Section=ALL

1085565,ca.proc.d.1936-03-19.8.1.5,1936-03-19,b4773d7c-fb30-477a-9d14-c076e60905ac,ca.m.9274,Mr. CHURCH:,,WAYS AND MEANS,CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT,,Some of them have gone to the United States. Others have had their mortgages foreclosed, and others have left the city, with the result that some of them have lost their homes which were located in the riding of the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Spence) and others in the northwest that I used to represent now represented by the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol).

The International Harvester Company has been referred to by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Wilton). As I see it this company might as well close up its factory in Hamilton, manufacture in Chicago, and ship its agricultural implements into Canada, so avoiding the high taxation put on by this parliament and by provincial and municipal authorities. It might as well close its Hamilton plant and manufacture in Chicago' under sweated labour conditions and child labour. The free trade and semi-free trade policies here will sooner or later see the end of these industries in Canada. In examining this item let us not forget the lessons of history. In the early eighties the city of Chicago, then the headquarters of the harvester industry, was known as the third largest Canadian city in the world; our industrial workers driven out of Canada by unemployment such as now exists, found employment there. As the result of the change of policy of the Conservatives these American factories had to establish plants in Canada. Industrial workers in our cities and towns benefited accordingly; so did the farmers.

I may say that I advocate in connection with the agricultural industry a policy of protection, beneficial to the farmer and to these industrial corporations, such as the International Harvester, which produce agricultural implements. The policy of protection I proposed in this house in 1924 is a national policy, protecting the farmer from exorbitant prices for his farm implements. Surely a national policy will not allow a Canadian farmer or any other consumer to be charged high prices for his farm implements. A truly national policy will provide an excise duty that will put into the national treasury every cent charged on agricultural implements, automobiles or any other product manufactured under protection at a price that represents fair wages to the workmen and fair profits to the manufacturers. I know that this proposal will be laughed at by the hon. member for North Huron (Mr. Deachman) and others as paternalism, but I would rather have paternalism along these lines of protecting the farmer against a high price for his implements than the paternalism of the Winnipeg grain exchange and the carryover people. Paternalism like that would be far better than the grain exchanges abuses we have. The only chance the Canadian manufacturer ever had to show what he can do in the way of mass production of ploughs and articles of that kind was during the war. He has never had a chance since. I am not pleading for protection merely for the manufacturer's sake but for Canada's sake, because I believe that protection should protect the consumer against unjustly high prices just as much as the manufacturer from unjust and unfair competition.

We have seen imports flowing into Canada for many years past and they now amount to a large sum of money. We have seen high duties and low duties. The more I consider this particular problem the more I believe that this industry needs adequate protection, because after all is said and done, it is one of Canada's oldest industries and it has flourished under protection. an impression that apparently prevails as stated by the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) in Hansard at page 821:

It is well known that we in the maritime provinces and Newfoundland produce practically all the lobsters in the world. We have the finest lobsters that are found anywhere. The only lobster, I believe, that is found' outside of Canada is one called the spiny lobster, which in reality is not a lobster at all.
As a matter of fact the United States produce as many lobsters as we export to them. Their production in recent years was as follows:

The year 1933 was the last year for which I could get the figures. The total exports of lobsters to the United States in 1934, the last year for which I could obtain the figures, amounted to 9,744,000 pounds. So that the statement made by the hon. member for Royal that lobsters were found only in the waters off the Canadian coast, to say t/he least is not according to the record. One-third of the exports of lobsters from Canada comes from a district in my constituency extending forty-five miles in length, and in 1934 the exports totalled 3,623,000 pounds. The second proviso of the reduction in the S3 excise tax provided for by section 601 (c) (6) of the Revenue Act of 1932 relates to a decision with respect to the application of the tax on timber six inches by six inches or larger in cross section. The provisions of this section of the Revenue Act of 1932 relate only to lumber and not to timber. It has been held by the United States customs court that timber refers to wood six inches by six inches or larger in cross section and lumber refers to wood sawn into boards, planks, et cetera, and of smaller dimensions. The treasury department is appealing this decision, but if it should be ruled that the revenue tax does not apply to timber six inches by six inches or larger, the second proviso referred to will have the effect of removing this class of lumber from the concessions granted in respect to paragraph 401 of the Tariff Act of 1930. In other words, the duty on this class of lumber shall not be less than SI per thousand feet board measure, but the second part of the proviso provides also that the duty shall not be at any time greater than S2 per thousand feet board measure, or the same duty as would have applied if this lumber were not excluded from the revenue tax by a decision of the United States customs court.

(Text) Before article IV passes I want to say just two or three words about this treaty in an effort to counteract some of the remarks made yesterday, especially by the hon. member for London (Mr. Betts). Referring to cream, the hon. member said that it would not make any difference or provide any benefit because the present United States duty of 35 cents on cream is too high. Let me give you the actual figures to show what has already happened under this treaty. Prior to 1930 the eastern townships of Quebec, the dairy sections, had been shipping gallons and gallons of cream to the United States, but that traffic was cut off by the action of the United States government in placing a duty of 56| cents against that commodity. Under this new arrangement made by the present government that duty has been reduced to 35 cents. The hon. member for London said that it would not benefit the farmers. I have figures secured by the hon. member for Stanstead, representing one of the eastern townships, and as he is not in the house I will quote them. The first shipment from the eastern townships, from the counties of Sherbrooke, Compton and Stanstead, under the new agreement, went to the United States on February 17 of this year, after a period of five years in which not a gallon had been sent to that market. What is the situation to-day? The present duty of 35 cents a gallon, representing a consider-12739-80

able reduction from the duty that had prevailed before, has meant to the farmers of Dixville, Bamston and Paquetteville from 26 to 29 cents per pound butter fat net, which is about 2 cents in excess of the Canadian price at the present time. If the American price should rise, shipments of cream will naturally increase. But the agreement has another most important bearing on our trade relations, especially in its effect on the dairy sections of Canada. Had it not been for the price which was being paid for American cream and our shipments to the United States -it is only in the last five weeks that we have started shipping again-the Canadian price would probably have dropped one or two cents per pound lower for butter fat, though it is bad enough as it is. This new shipment of cream to the United States has resulted in a better price to our Canadian farmers.

Everyone in the house knows my business, and as a manufacturer and lumberman I say that everything that this government can do to increase the purchasing power of the primary producers in Canada will benefit our manufacturers; indeed, that is the only salvation of the manufacturers. I believe that the supporters of the policy followed by the last administration during the past five years will admit to-day the serious consequences of their effort, for the first time in the history of Canada, to maintain extreme protection. The consequence was that employment diminished and there were few manufacturers who could make profits, so that conditions were worse than we had ever before experienced. If we can increase the purchasing power of our farmers and lumbermen, our miners and fishermen, it will be easy enough to double the flow of Canadian manufactured products to the consumers. As a manufacturer, I say that we would rather have less profits proportionately; we would rather have more business at a lower rate of profit.

I was quite surprised to hear the criticisms especially on items that had been reduced, going into the United States. Have we ever stopped to think that this trade with the United States is the best that we could have, considering the fact that the President of the United States was not authorized to concede more than a fifty per cent reduction? Speaking of cream, if this treaty had gone into effect, as it should have done, in 1911, cream would have been on the free list to-day. But we turned down the reciprocity agreement in 1911; and speaking from the standpoint of the farmers in the eastern townships of

Quebec, I can assure you that we are mighty glad to get the reduction to 35 cents, and I hope that this agreement in its present form will serve as a basis for future negotiations which will restore a greater volume of trade to us and be of benefit not only to the farmers but to all the people of Canada. It is for that reason that I support it.

1085750,ca.proc.d.1936-03-19.8.1.190,1936-03-19,intervention,,,,WAYS AND MEANS,CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT,,No prohibitions, import or customs quotas, import licences, or any other form of quantitative regulation, whether or not operated in connection with any agency of centralized control, shall be imposed by Canada on the importation or sale of any article the growth, produce or manufacture of the United States of America enumerated and described in schedule I, nor by the TJn'ted States of America on the importation or sale of any article the growth, produce or manufacture of Canada enumerated and described in schedule II, except as specifically provided' for in the said schedules.

The foregoing provision shall not apply to quantitative restrictions in whatever form imposed by either country on the importation or sale of any article the growth, produce or manufacture of the country in conjunction with governmental measures operating to regulate or control the production, market supply, or prices of like domestic articles, or tending to increase the labour costs of production of such articles. Whenever the government of either country proposes to establish or change any restriction authorized by this paragraph, it shall give notice thereof in writing to the other government and shall afford such other government an opportunity within thirty days after receipt of such notice to consult with it in respect of the proposed action; and if an agreement with respect thereto is not reached within thirty days following receipt of the aforesaid notice, the government which proposes to take such action shall be free to do so at any time thereafter, and the other government shall be free within fifteen days after such action is taken to terminate this agreement in its entirety on thirty days' written notice.

the point where he is prepared to raise any kind of objection, whether it be relevant or otherwise. Certainly nothing could better illustrate the position taken by the opposition towards the agreement than what has been said by the hon. member. Along with other hon. members in his party, he has stressed over and over again that the agreement is likely to be injurious to Canada. In the next breath he objects because there is a means of terminating its provisions inside of three years. I cannot understand why in the administration of the agreement the hon. member should not impute as fair and honourable motives to the government of the United States as he does to the government of Canada. He speaks as though the people of the United States were a sharp bargaining lot, and leaves the suggestion that they are going to do something which would give them an unfair advantage in the agreement as time goes on. In the same breath he opposes a clause in the agreement which would give Canada the opportunity to terminate it, in the event of anything of the kind happening. These clauses have been included not for the benefit of the United States government or for that of the Canadian government, but for the benefit of both, to see that what is fair and proper is done on each side. If there is anything at all in the hon. member's suggestion that the people of the United States are going to be so sharp, or that they are going to do this and that which is unfair, then I think we have the strongest of all reasons for having in the agreement a clause which will enable the government of Canada to terminate it should such circumstance arise. I am sure that when the hon. member reads what he has said he will find that from beginning to end his argument is contradictory.

1085820,ca.proc.d.1936-03-19.8.1.260,1936-03-19,5f73217f-27d7-4bec-9943-554ca0daade8,ca.m.7834,Mr. HEAPS:,,WAYS AND MEANS,CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT,,This article is very wide indeed and it appears to affect only half of the trade between the two countries. Either government has the right to cancel the whole agreement. If the United States thought they were at a disadvantage in some particular respect owing to exchange conditions, they could terminate the whole agreement in thirty days. It is true that there must be certain negotiations in the meantime; nevertheless it seems to me that there should have been something more definite in an article of this sort defining the meaning of the word ""wide"" in the term ""wide variation"" in the first line. if it considers the variation so substantial as to prejudice the industries or commerce of the country-

1085823,ca.proc.d.1936-03-19.8.1.263,1936-03-19,4430053b-1f47-481d-9354-7a7535f63be9,ca.m.8546,Sir GEORGE PERLEY:,,WAYS AND MEANS,CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT,,"Yesterday my hon. friend from St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) explained carefully the difficulty with regard to the legislation now pending in the United States congress with respect to the distillers of this country, under which they might be forced to give up the benefits of this agreement unless they could put up a vast sum of money as security for costs in the cases which the United States government is threatening to bring against them for damages. That I consider one of the most serious things discussed in this house with respect to the agreement, because undoubtedly the provision for the reduction in the duty on Canadian whiskey and spirits going into the United States is one that may be of great benefit to Canada. I asked the Prime Minister yesterday whether there was any clause in this agreement which would enable us to terminate the agreement if the
Canada-U\S. Trade Agreement

United States should pass that legislation and in that way prevent our distillers from exporting spirits to the United States under the agreement. He told me he thought it could be done under the escape clause. I have been looking this over carefully and I thought it might be done under article XI, if the government of either country-

-adopts any measure which, even though it does not conflict with the terms of this agreement, is considered by the government of the other country to have the effect of nullifying or impairing any object of the agreement.

That is certainly what the legislation in question would do. The only right given Canada under this article XI would be in that event to make representations and proposals to the other government with a view to effecting a mutually satisfactory adjustment of the matter. These various clauses which allow the denunciation of the treaty on comparatively short notice for various minor reasons do not seem to give a similar power with regard to this very important matter. That is, if they pass legislation in the United States which in effect nullifies the agreement, what are Canada's rights in the matter? And if the negotiations with the United States do not bring about such a change in their policy as would be reasonable and satisfactory to us, have we any power to put an end to this agreement if our reasonable representations are not effective?

Except as otherwise provided in the second paragraph of this article, the provisions of this agreement relating to the treatment to be accorded by Canada and the United States of America, respectively, to the commerce of the other country, shall not apply to the Philippine Islands, the Virgin Islands, American Samoa, the Island of Guam or to the Panama Canal Zone.

1085843,ca.proc.d.1936-03-19.8.1.283,1936-03-19,intervention,,,,WAYS AND MEANS,CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT,,The present agreement shall be ratified by His Majesty the King of Great Britain, Ireland and the British dominions beyond the Seas, Emperor of India, in respect of the Dominion of Canada and shall be proclaimed by the President of the United States of America.

The provisions of Article I and of Articles III and IV, respectively, shall, subject to the reservations and exceptions elsewhere provided for in this agreement, be applied by Canada and the United States of America, on and after January 1. 1936, pending ratification of the agreement in respect of Canada as provided in the first paragraph of this article.

The entire agreement shall come into force on the day of the exchange of the proclamation and ratification at Ottawa. The agreement shall remain in force until December 31, 1938, subject to the provisions of Article VII, Article X and Article XIV.

Unless at least six months before December 31, 1938, the government of either country shall have given to the other government notice of intention to terminate the agreement on that date, the agreement shall remain in force thereafter, subject to the provisions of Article VII, Article X and Article XIV, until six months from such time as the government of either country shall have given notice to the other government.

1085864,ca.proc.d.1936-03-19.8.2.1.5,1936-03-19,28eb2ff4-b1a9-437b-87d1-34c64f68f258,ca.m.7788,Mr. ROGERS:,Minister of Labour,WAYS AND MEANS,EMPLOYMENT COMMISSION,ADMINISTRATION OP UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOR NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE,As the resolution indicates, the purpose of the legislation which is to follow is to create an agency which will facilitate cooperation between the federal government, provincial governments, municipalities, industrial corporations, labour organizations and social welfare agencies in dealing constructively with the problem of unemployment and relief. It is recognized that unemployment is a matter of national concern and calls for an organized national effort. It is the opinion of the government that such effort can be most effectively made through the advice and assistance of a national commission. Provision will also be made for the appointment of a national advisory committee, including representatives of industrial, occupational and social welfare organizations. It may also be appropriate to observe that at the dominion-provincial conference held last December the proposal to establish a national commission on unemployment and relief received the unanimous approval of the provincial delegation. The hon. member for Argenteuil (Sir George Perley) suggested that an extended explanation of the bill might be given at this time. I believe it is not customary to make such an explanation at this stage. There will be ample opportunity for full discussion when the bill is introduced, and I think hon. members would wish to have the provisions of the bill before them prior to such discussion. So far as the government is concerned, we are most anxious to expedite this legislation, and are therefore of the opinion that the resolution itself should be proceeded with as quickly as possible in order that the bill to follow may be introduced.

1085947,ca.proc.d.1936-03-19.12.1.3,1936-03-19,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals,NATIONAL HARBOURS BOARD,PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL OF PUBLIC HARBOURS,,The measure proposed by this resolution has to do with the management and financial control of the national harbours of Halifax, Saint John, Quebec, Chicoutimi, Three Rivers, Montreal and Vancouver. Until recently these ports were administered by separate harbour commissioners, each commission composed of three men chosen from the immediate locality. It was found in practice that this form of control was inefficient and exceedingly costly to the federal government. During 1931 a survey of the national ports of Canada was conducted by Sir Alexander Gibb who, after a close study of the operations of each harbour, recommended that local commissions be abolished and that the control be centralized in Ottawa. His report was made in January, 1932, but no action was taken on it, and the administrative weaknesses and undesirable practices to which he called attention have continued in increasing measure during the years that have followed.

Shortly after this government took office the local board were replaced by a central board located at Ottawa, this board being appointed the harbour commissioners for each of the seven ports. To this extent control of the harbours has already been centralized in Ottawa, but satisfactory results can be obtained only when new legislation is provided that will make possible proper accounting and adequate control of the finances of each port, and the necessary expert direction of the businesses conducted by the various port managements. The importance of the bill will be appreciated from the fact that the property assets of the seven ports brought within the jurisdiction of the proposed commission represent to-day a capital
investment of $176,000,000. Their annual revenues have varied from $7,000,000 to $9,000,000, and their annual expenditures from $10,000,000 to $23,000,000 per annum over the past six or seven years.

The proposed bill will provide for the creation of a national harbours board with headquarters at Ottawa, which, under a minister of the crown, will be responsible for the administration, maintenance and control of the seven ports already referred to as well as any other harbour property which the governor in council may transfer to the board for administration. It is intended that each of the three members constituting the central harbours board shall be an expert in some branch of port activity, and that engineering works which have heretofore been under the direction of small local staffs will in future be carried out with the best engineering skill available in the government services. Local management will devolve upon competent port managers with the proper background of experience, whose duty it will be to develop the same local contacts that were formerly maintained by the separate harbour boards.

The financial control of each port will be under the direction of the comptroller of the treasury and subject to audit by the auditor general of Canada. The accounting for each port will, however, be carried out at the port, and funds earned at one port will not be diverted for use elsewhere.

This bill will provide for the amalgamation of the seven harbour corporations, and the change is intended to ensure a substantial saving in operating costs, a budgeted control of expenditure, and a coordinated and greatly improved direction of port administration and engineering practice.

,Liberal,,Clarence Decatur Howe,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb&Language=E&Section=ALL

1086010,ca.proc.d.1936-03-19.13.10,1936-03-19,f88a7275-f7f4-407e-9d45-89d5300f2919,ca.m.9510,Mr. POULIOT:,,DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE,,,But some icicles are not

put into the pot for melting, and one of the icicles is the five per cent cut. The man receives so much less. Well, in that there must be an element of fairness, which means that if the small salaried man, the under-dog, has to make the sacrifice of that $5, another man should not receive privileged treatment. The answer of the government was a half truth. It is impossible to pay the salary of another man from a sum of money which is not actually paid, but with all the savings that are made by cutting the salaries of these small salaried men big sums are accumulated, and those plums are given to privileged fellows who can dip into the melting pot with a very big ladle. Now, when hon. members understand how the matter is worked everyone will be scandalized. I shall explain it in detail in order that no one may miss the point. I want to make myself very clear, for there is nothing more difficult to prove or establish than elementary truths and elementary facts. How can we prove that the sun shines in the daytime? You say, Look at the sun. But to prove this, is a very hard proposition. It does not take a very subtle man to understand this; all I ask from anyone is just a few moments of attention, and the less I am called to order the sooner will the explanation be complete.

Well, take this small fellow; he is entitled to $100. The axe comes, the resolution of this house to cut the salaries, and $5 comes off his $100. He does not receive it. That employee in the Department of National Revenue, or in any government department, is the man who is deprived of the five dollar bill which he might require to send his boy to school, to buy a suit of clothes for his small child, to buy some kindling wood, to buy food or for other purposes. When a man can rely on the state, not lean on it, and when he realizes that while working for his country he receives fair consideration, although his remuneration may be small, he will give his best service. He is entitled to the same consideration as the man who has more pull, or who can pull more strings.

That action was taken by the Henry administration, and was denounced by the humble member for Temiscouata and other hon. members, when we sat in opposition. country he says, ""I am ready to make that sacrifice. I need the five dollar bill, but if everyone is treated in the same way I will gladly give it. However, if there are others who receive more than they need I do not see why I should be deprived of what I need properly to bring up my children.""

Some people have said that the farmers favour a decrease in salaries, and that they would be pleased by such decrease. How many bags of potatoes must the old fellow sell in order to send a five dollar bill to his son?

We set the example. When a mistake was made by the late Tory government in Ontario it had a bad effect in that province, but it was worse when the same procedure was followed by this House of Commons. The import duty for the last complete year, 193435, is S36,042.97; excise taxes amounted to $262,512.03, making a total of $298,555. I would point out that excise taxes should not be taken into account at all because they can be paid at a distance just as well as nearby. The only one of these figures that counts is the import duty, and there the important matter to look at is the number of entries. There were only 579 import entries in

1934-35, which means that the officer there was entering less than two per day, on an average. The hon. gentleman will understand that when a customs collector has only two entries to make a day, this gives the public the idea that a government job does not mean anything but is a pure sinecure. It is a shame to have these positions in existence if they can possibly be wiped out. We have just been told that the number of customs ports in the United States is very little more than half the number in Canada, notwithstanding the enormously greater business of the neighbouring country. There is also this fact to remember, that in the United States the customs ports are frontier ports, whereas in Canada we have a large number of inland ports.

Neither party can escape responsibility for the condition that has grown up in this country. Local pressure upon members has led to the creation of a large number of small ports throughout Canada. That we know to be a matter of fact. The purpose has been a play to local pride, in a measure, and also to provide positions for political friends as collectors or subcollectors at such small ports, but the expenditure in the aggregate is large. When we are

asked to turn to the revenue side it must be remembered that when you close up a port you do not lose any public revenue; that revenue is collected at some other port. From the standpoint of administration it is obvious that administration of customs laws, the tariff and the regulations will be much more uniform and effectual if the administration is in the hands of trained and experienced officials such as are to be found in the larger ports, and such as, in the very nature of things one cannot have in the smaller ones.

I approve the policy of closing, as speedily as conditions permit, the smaller ports. The revenue will not suffer, nor, I venture to say, will any great inconvenience be occasioned to merchants or, for that matter, to manufacturers in such small towns in which ports may be closed. In the United States they manage to get along very well, apparently, with frontier ports only. In passing goods through the customs apparently there would be no difficulty in having agents in large ports like Vancouver, Winnipeg, Toronto, Montreal and so on, to conduct the business expeditiously and satisfactorily for the consignees.

1086108,ca.proc.d.1936-03-19.13.108,1936-03-19,396d7d47-d79c-4aea-bf33-18c3e7b199e3,ca.m.9501,Mr. ILSLEY:,Minister of National Revenue,DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE,,,Since 1904 or 1907, I forget the exact year, we have had in our customs tariff a clause which is popularly known as the dumping clause. This was introduced when Mr. Fielding was Minister of Finance. The principle of the clause is that if exporters in foreign countries sell goods to persons in Canada at less than the home market value in the country of origin, the importer in this country is charged in addition to the regular duty, what is known as a special or dumping duty. That makes it necessary for the department and for our collectors to ascertain these facts. Whether or not they have the right to do that is not for our department to say; the function of our department is merely to administer the law as we find it. We have to find out by the best means at our command whether goods are being invoiced to this country at prices less than the home market value. We have to find out what is the home market value. That is not as simple as it might appear to be. It is sometimes very difficult to ascertain the fair home market value in the country of origin under conditions
Supply-National Revenue
similar to those under which the sale is made to the importer in Canada. For this reason we have to have investigators of values in foreign countries. That is the first part of their duties.

As I indicated a moment ago, there is another part to check co9ts of production abroad. This becomes necessary because of a provision in our Customs Act, not the customs tariff, which says that the value for duty purposes shall not be less than the cost of production in the country of origin plus a reasonable advance for selling costs and profit. Therefore, we have a very difficult duty to perform in attempting to ascertain in some way costs of production in foreign countries. It is very difficult even to find out costs of production in our own country as they vary from firm to firm, from place to place and from time to time. Nevertheless we have to do our best to get these costs of production in foreign countries so long as that law remains on our statute books. This is a second part of the duties of these investigators of values in foreign countries.

memorandum on the arrangement with

Ontario. That arrangement has not been finally completed, but I anticipate that there will be no difficulty in coming to an agreement since the principles are all settled. The Ontario Income Tax Act imposes a tax on all persons resident in Ontario and individuals carrying on business in Ontario-For this purpose the Ontario act has followed as closely as may be the dominion law. The Ontario law imposes rates that are equal to one-half of the general schedule of rates contained in the dominion act. The personal exemptions and allowances for dependents are the same for both acts. The income subject to tax under the dominion law is also subject to tax under the Ontario law, with two variations:

column2: An addition of the tax free 1937 dominion bond interest income. That is taxable in Ontario; we do not tax it, but they do.
The dominion tax payable is a deduction from the Ontario income, before determining the amount of income subject to the Ontario tax. That is a very important consideration.

column1: It might be well to mention that the Ontario act does not impose any of the other taxes contained in the dominion act, such as the surtax on investment income, the five per cent additional tax on incomes in excess of $5,000, the gift tax or the corporation tax. I think hon. members understand that the Ontario law is an individual income tax law, not a corporation income tax law. We get approximately half our income tax revenue from corporations throughout Canada.

The administration of the Ontario act is substantially in the control of the dominion commissioner of income tax in the same manner and to the same extent that that officer administers the dominion act. The' return of income made by the individual for both dominion and Ontario purposes is on one form. The forms supplying information covering salaries or wages of employees, dividendrS, ownership certificates, beneficiaries-of estates, interest paid to fully registered bondholders and other information, are used both for dominion and Ontario purposes, thereby eliminating the necessity of the persons required to make such returns having to do the same thing twice, once for dontinion purposes and again for Ontario purposes.

Without detailing the numerous different forms it may be said that these have been redrafted to show clearly dominion and Ontario assessments, together with collections, separately on the same form, thus saving time, material, space and equipment. The receipt forms have been redrafted so that

the amounts paid by the taxpayer for dominion purposes or Ontario purposes can be clearly designated on the receipt and therefore one receipt is adaptable for either purpose. The notice of assessment has been redrafted so that the taxpayer knows precisely the amount of his indebtedness and the exact standing of his account for both dominion and Ontario purposes.

The province will be required to pay its share of the supplies, added equipment, travelling expenses incurred and salaries occasioned by possible additions to the staff. There are seven dominion district offices in Ontario and approximately 85,000 individual taxpayers, for whom separate accounts must be opened and further general ledger records maintained. ,Conservative (1867-1942),,William Allen Walsh,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=d8b00805-fbe7-407f-8512-1e9d5594ebe9&Language=E&Section=ALL

1086185,ca.proc.d.1936-03-19.13.185,1936-03-19,4ec07e21-5e6c-41f8-9fa6-c6cbf37549e8,ca.m.3404,Mr. MacNICOL:,,DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE,,,I wanted to ask the minister a question, not particularly in connection with this last item. A former revenue officer of the department, came to see me, a

man who was employed by the department at the time of the Mont Blanc explosion in Halifax harbour, I believe in 1915. While on duty he was blown into the water; several of his family were killed; his house was blown away-he lived on the shore near where the ship blew up; he now Lives in Toronto-and ever since that time he has been trying to get some redress from the department. The doctor ordered him to move away because his wife could not bear to live in the vicinity where members of the family were killed. I have been wondering why the department will not place him in the revenue service again. I will give the minister particulars, and he can let me have information about the matter at his convenience.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,John Ritchie MacNicol,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=4ec07e21-5e6c-41f8-9fa6-c6cbf37549e8&Language=E&Section=ALL

,Liberal,,James Lorimer Ilsley,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=396d7d47-d79c-4aea-bf33-18c3e7b199e3&Language=E&Section=ALL
